title: Effects of illuminance and correlated color temperature on emotional responses and lighting adjustment behaviors
research_question: RQ1. Will self-reported arousal and emotional valence levels be affected by initial illuminance and CCT? Furthermore, will these effects be moderated by gender? RQ2. Will adjusted lighting preference be affected by the initial lighting conditions? Furthermore, will these effects be moderated by gender? RQ3. Will the order effects of the presented lighting conditions affect the lighting adjustment behavior? RQ4. Finally, we were interested in determining if consistent individual user profiles could be developed in regard to lighting adjustment behaviors.

participants.description: 27 healthy adults (16 women, 11 men), age 18-64 years (mean 24.16, SD 8.09), associated with Cornell University (23 undergraduate students, 4 graduate students/faculty). Majority used eyeglasses (59%), 75% difficulty seeing far, 19% difficulty seeing close. Majority identified as students/researchers (67%), programmers (25%).
participants.recruitment: convenience sampling method (word-of-mouth and announcements on departmental e-mail lists)

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Virtual office environment (3.7 m × 7.2 m x 3.0 m) created in Autodesk 3ds Max and Unreal Engine 4.26. Presented via Meta Quest 2-HMD (1832 × 1920 pixels per eye, 90° horizontal FOV, 90 Hz refresh rate). 17 distinct lighting conditions (7 CCTs: 1500 K-7500 K; 7 illuminance levels: 45 lx-780 lx) pre-programmed using DIALux Evo and Philips CoreLine Recessed luminaires.

mechanisms: Anchor effects: initial lighting conditions bias subsequent preferences and adjustment behavior.
Participant adaptation to the VR display, leading to increased light sensitivity.
Fatigue from repeated trials, prompting gravitation toward less arousing light conditions.
Habituation to lighting conditions over time, leading to adjustments towards lower values.
Individual differences in response profiles, potentially influenced by demographic factors like gender.
implementation_implications: Lighting designs should consider customization options for illuminance and CCT to enhance user satisfaction and wellbeing, especially given individual and gender-based variations.
Spaces intended to promote arousal (e.g., offices) can benefit from brighter lighting, while spaces for healing/calm (e.g., patient rooms) may benefit from more subdued lighting.
Designers should use caution when applying CCT for intended emotional impacts, especially when moving away from mid-range CCT values (3500-6000 K).
VR simulations are valuable for assessing lighting design impacts on users in the AEC industry, allowing efficient exploration and testing of various lighting scenarios.
Initial lighting conditions should be carefully chosen to balance occupant satisfaction and energy conservation, aligning with sustainability goals.
Future research should explore longer exposure times and objective physiological response data to triangulate self-reports.

limitations: VR systems do not provide a full dynamic range compared to real-world lighting, limiting generalizability to real-world contexts.
Findings may differ across VR systems or tone mapping algorithms.
Limited sample size and convenience recruitment method, limiting generalizability to broader populations and inability to account for variables like age, geographic background, or sleep schedules.
Data loss due to technical glitches led to a higher-than-expected attrition rate, impacting sample size.
